newsitem.title: JAPAN: Matsushita half-year profit surges on weak yen.
newsitem.headline: Matsushita half-year profit surges on weak yen.

text.p: Giant consumer electronics group Matsushita Electric Industrial Co reported on Tuesday a surge in half-year profits helped by the weak yen.
Matsushita -- whose products are sold under the National, Panasonic and Technics brand names -- raised its full-year group profit forecast, but said economic uncertainties still cloud its outlook.

Matsushita reported a group net profit of 42.6 billion yen ($383 million) for the April through September period, a turnaround from a 132.9 billion yen ($1.19 billion) loss in the same period a year before.
When the effects of the 1995 sale of an 80 percent stake in U.S. film maker MCA Inc were excluded, net profits jumped 36 percent year-on-year, Matsushita said.

"We suffered sagging prices in overseas markets. The price declines slashed group profits by as much as 67.5 billion yen ($608 million) during the six months, but the lower yen helped to offset some of them," Motoi Matsuda, Matsushita's executive director, told a news conference.
The weak yen, for instance, more than tripled half-year profits at information equipment unit Matsushita-Kotobuki Electronics Industries Ltd, which last year was battered by the strong yen.
Matsushita-Kotobuki sells hard disk drives (HDDs), CD-ROM drives and other information products, mostly overseas.
Overall, the group's sales of information-related equipment grew 22 percent, aided also by a mobile phone boom in Japan, Matsuda said.
Only its electronic components business, which includes computer chips, suffered slower growth, Matsuda said.
Matsushita raised the group's full-year pretax profit forecast to 280 billion yen ($2.52 billion) from its May projection of 270 billion yen ($2.43 billion).
This would be an increase of 16 percent from 1995/96 when the effects of MCA stocks are excluded.
The forecasts are based on an exchange rate of 108 yen to the dollar, compared with 89 yen a year earlier.
But the company said sagging prices of computer-related goods and uncertainty in the domestic market cast a shadow over its outlook for the second half.
"An improvement in the computer-related products market is yet to be seen. We are also worried whether we can achieve the domestic sales target," Matsuda said.
